Title: One killed, 15 wounded as car hits crowd near Berlin Gay Pride
Article:
BERLIN: At least one person was killed and around 15 wounded after a car hit the crowd on the outskirts of the Berlin Gay Pride parade, police said Saturday.
"A vehicle entered the Tiergarten park and hit several people and injured them" just before 10pm (2000 GMT), police posted on social media, later adding that they were hunting for the occupants of the car.
Police spokesman Florian Nath said some of the survivors had been "seriously" injured and were being treated by the emergency services.
Police told AFP they had found the car they thought had been involved in the incident abandoned in the Tiergarten park.
The Gay Pride event was cut short and police told participants to "Go home, please" and sealed off the area where the people were injured.
An eyewitness by the main Pride stage at Brandenburg Gate said the crowd complied with the request to leave and head away from the park shortly at around 11pm.
The programme at the main stage had been scheduled to continue until midnight.
An AFP journalist in the area saw at least 10 emergency service vehicles at the scene and a tent set up in the road.
Police officers could be seen patrolling the huge area of the park.
VIOLENT ATTACKS
Earlier Saturday, hundreds of thousands of people took part in the event, called Christopher Street Day in Germany.
The march ended next to the Brandenburg Gate, which has been the venue for concerts since Friday.
Germany has in recent years seen several violent attacks at public spaces, including a stabbing in February 2025 at Berlin's Holocaust memorial, a stone's throw from the scene of Saturday's incident.
A 20-year-old Syrian man named only as Wassim Al M. was jailed in March for 13 years for that attack, in which a Spanish tourist was seriously injured.
Last month Taleb Jawad al-Abdulmohsen, a 51-year-old Saudi psychiatrist, was sentenced to life in prison for killing six people and wounding more than 300.
He drove a rented SUV through a crowded Christmas market in 2024 in the easter city of Magedburg.
Abdulmohsen was an anti-Islam activist and his testimony at his trial was sometimes incoherent and riddled with conspiracy theories and fringe far-right ideas.
The deadliest such attack in recent years was a truck rampage at a Berlin Christmas market in December 2016 that killed 12 people.

Title: Parents divided over merit system for students who report bullying, drugs [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:   Parents are divided over a proposal to introduce a merit system for students who report bullying, extortion or drug involvement in schools, raising concerns that their children could later be targeted.
Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia (Page) chairman Datin Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim said while there were concerns about  violence in schools, parents were also worried about how their children would be protected when they report crimes.
"With concerns about severe school violence, gang infiltration and drug use, many parents welcome any measure that encourages breaking the silence.
"But among those who oppose, the primary worry  is whistleblower  protection.
"In serious cases involving drugs or extortion rings, a merit point is not worth the physical safety risk to their child," she told the
New Straits Times
.
Bukit Aman Crime Prevention and Community Safety Department director Datuk Noor Hisam Nordin had said the proposal was among several measures put forward to strengthen crime prevention in schools.
He said it  would help school authorities detect misconduct early while cultivating a strong culture of reporting among students.
But Azimah said reporting criminal activities  should stem from civic duty, moral obligation and maintaining a safe learning environment, rather than a transactional point-scoring mechanism.
However, National Parent-Teacher Association  president Associate Professor Datuk Dr Mohamad Ali Hasan said the police proposal should be welcomed, provided clear operational guidelines are established.
"It is an idea that should be encouraged and the practicalities should be finalised," he told the
New Straits Times
, adding that strict safeguards must be implemented to ensure the system is not abused by any party.
Ali added that a merit system would instil greater student confidence in school disciplinary processes and policing mechanisms, reassuring them that reported incidents will be acted upon promptly.
"Students will become more cautious of their actions, knowing that misbehaviour could be reported and ultimately jeopardise their academic performance. It will deter students from bullying and gangsterism."
Ali added that the initiative would also encourage parents and guardians to play a more active role in moulding their children's character.
He  suggested introducing a complementary demerit system with penalties to deter repeated disciplinary breaches.
However, he said, mechanisms must be developed to prevent students from submitting false or malicious reports.
The police proposal comes in the wake of   violent incidents in schools.
On July 6, a 15-year-old  female student suffered injuries after being stabbed by a classmate at a secondary school in Banting.
The suspect was charged with attempted murder.
Days later, a 13-year-old  male student allegedly pointed a penknife at a schoolmate and chased him for about 50m at a secondary school in Alor Gajah, Melaka.
A teacher managed to persuade the student to hand over the weapon and no injuries were reported.

Title: Lessons from Iran: Malaysia must shape nuclear narrative early
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:  As tensions between Iran and the United States continue to affect the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global energy shipping lane, the crisis has reminded many countries, including Malaysia, that a nuclear programme is never judged on local and technical grounds alone.
For Teheran, uranium enrichment has long been intertwined with its confrontation with Washington, drawing scrutiny over inspections, sanctions, maritime security and accusations over the direction of its nuclear programme.
Even as diplomacy appears to be gaining ground, the episode shows how quickly a civilian nuclear question can become part of a wider geopolitical contest.
Dr Habibreza Arzani, cultural counsellor at Iran's embassy in Kuala Lumpur, said Iran's experience showed that nuclear development was often judged not only on technical grounds, but also through the political narratives built around a country's scientific advancement.
He said Malaysia could draw lessons from this by ensuring that a nuclear plan is communicated from the start as a peaceful, developmental and transparent national project.
"The most significant lesson is that technical transparency alone is sometimes not enough if the geopolitical narrative is controlled by others.
"Addressing these complex questions requires looking beyond mere technicalities and understanding the broader civilisational frameworks and the global war of narratives that often surround scientific advancement in the developing world."
He said Malaysia should invest early in public diplomacy, legal transparency and international communication before any civilian nuclear programme could be framed negatively by outside actors.
He said Malaysia should also build its own academic and technical expertise, rather than depend entirely on foreign turnkey solutions.
He said a nuclear programme should be deeply integrated into national scientific institutions so that Malaysia was not only a buyer of technology, but also a country with its own knowledge base and technical confidence.
On regional perception, Arzani said Malaysia could reduce external anxieties by framing any future programme within Asean's energy security goals, rather than presenting it only as a national ambition.
He said international safeguards, inspections and diplomacy would be important bridges of trust between a sovereign country and the global community.
"In regions vulnerable to maritime choke-point disruptions, such as the Strait of Hormuz or the Strait of Malacca, nuclear power is a cornerstone of true energy independence."
Taylor's University international relations expert Dr Julia Roknifard said civilian nuclear energy often attracted geopolitical suspicion due to its dual-use nature.
"The suspicion around civilian nuclear energy stems from the concept of dual-use technology, as the same enrichment process that produces reactor fuel can also produce weapons-grade material."
But Malaysia should not be viewed through the same lens as countries with contested security records, she said, given its status as a signatory to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the Biological Weapons Convention and its domestic legal framework under the Strategic Trade Act.
"Malaysia should clearly state its goals, like access to medical isotopes, energy security and other valid reasons that other nuclear powers enjoy."
She said Malaysia should avoid allowing the debate to be framed as a choice between developing nuclear infrastructure and being seen as a proliferation concern.
"Malaysia should communicate that it views nuclear cooperation as a technical, civilian contract."
Asean-level confidence-building would be crucial as nuclear power was not only a domestic energy issue, but also a regional security and perception issue, she said.
"Malaysia could even lead Asean initiatives to establish a regional code of conduct for civilian nuclear transparency — shared notification of fuel shipments, joint disaster-response drills, and mutual International Atomic Energy Agency inspections."

Title: Clock ticking on Malaysia's nuclear future, says industry veteran
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:  Malaysia risks falling behind other countries if it continues to delay a decision on nuclear power, said veteran nuclear industry figure Raja Datuk Abdul Aziz Raja Adnan.
The former Atomic Energy Licensing Board director-general said the issue was no longer whether Malaysia had studied nuclear energy, but whether it had the political will to act on years of technical groundwork.
"I am at the final stage of my career and I want to see the next generation benefit. I will be very happy if everyone is informed before they make a decision. Do not make a decision emotionally."
Aziz, a former director of nuclear security and special assistant to the director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, said work completed around 2018 had already produced a feasibility study, although it would need to be updated against current realities.
He said the earlier work was done without a binding national commitment, allowing successive administrations to revisit the issue instead of making a firm decision.
He said the cost of waiting was no longer theoretical, as more countries in Asean, Africa and elsewhere were now looking seriously at nuclear energy.
He said Malaysia risked being pushed further down the queue for technology, vendors, expertise, training and industrial opportunities if it continued to delay a decision.
"We are not the only country looking at nuclear energy. If other countries decide to move with nuclear energy, we will have to compete for nuclear technology.
"The longer you wait, the more likely we are to lose the first-mover advantage."
Aziz, now principal advisor to eCEOs Sdn Bhd, said Malaysia's push into higher-value industries, particularly artificial intelligence and data centres, would require a stable and large-scale supply of electricity.
He said the first challenge for Malaysia was not to imagine a fully nuclear grid, but to introduce one plant safely and responsibly.
"Do not talk about 100 per cent. One is enough. We take one step at a time to see whether we can manage it safely."
He acknowledged that nuclear plants were capital intensive, with facilities potentially costing US$5 billion to US$10 billion, excluding supporting infrastructure.
However, he said, their long lifespan meant the economics had to be viewed over decades, rather than through short-term capital cost alone.
"If you stretch it to 60 years, after 20 years you may already get your return on investment," he said, adding that nuclear's levelised cost of electricity could be competitive if subsidies and hidden costs in other energy sources were properly accounted for.
On siting,  Aziz declined to identify any  location, saying the first plant must be placed where it was safest, most suitable and had strong public acceptance.
He said regulation and national public consultation were the government's responsibility, not the role of any project developer.
Malaysia had the industrial base to benefit from the wider nuclear ecosystem, he said, including in components and related supply chains, but could lose that opportunity if it remained outside the programme.
He said the country's climate commitments made the nuclear question more urgent, as Malaysia would still need reliable baseload power while pursuing its long-term emissions targets.
"We also have the Paris Agreement and climate targets. We need to achieve those targets by 2040 or 2050. That is a motivation.
"If not, we may have to return to coal."

Title: Syria bus crash kills at least 35
Article:
DAMASCUS: A crash between two passenger buses in a central-eastern desert region of Syria on Saturday killed at least 35 people, state media said.
News agency SANA, quoting a health ministry official, also said 30 others were injured in the "collision between two passenger buses on the Damascus-Deir Ezzor road."
The interior ministry said the crash was between "a bus carrying a number of internal security forces personnel and a civilian bus", without specifying how many of the casualties were from its forces.
State media broadcast footage of the crash, including images of a bus on fire and with debris strewn along the highway, and reported that military helicopters had been deployed to airlift casualties from the scene.
Emergency and disaster management minister Raed Al Saleh described the crash as "one of the deadliest road accidents in Syria in recent years in terms of the number of victims."
He said it "places a shared national responsibility on all of us to work to prevent such painful incidents from recurring", according to SANA.
"It also underscores the urgent need to address the accumulated challenges facing the country's road infrastructure, which is burdened by years of neglect and the damage inflicted on various public service sectors."
Earlier this month, five people were killed and dozens of others injured, most of them Lebanese, when a bus carrying pilgrims returning from Saudi Arabia overturned on a highway in southern Syria's Daraa province.
After years of civil war and neglect, Syria's infrastructure is crumbling and many of its roads are in need of repairs.
State television quoted the director of road transport in Damascus, Moaz Najjar, as saying that authorities "have directed that road maintenance in the eastern region be treated as a priority."
He added that "most roads are in a state of disrepair and have not undergone maintenance for the past 15 years."
Last year, at least 12 people were killed and several others injured when a bus collided with an oil tanker in northeastern Syria.
But Saturday's accident was one of the worst in recent years.
In 2020, at least 32 died when a fuel tanker crashed into two buses on a road between Damascus and Homs province.

Title: Groups warn against nuclear rush
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia must not rush into nuclear power without first answering hard questions on cost, safety, radioactive waste, foreign dependency and public accountability, consumer and environmental groups said.
Federation of Malaysian Consumers Associations chief executive officer Dr Saravanan Thambirajah said the group was not opposed to any technology simply because it was new or different.
However, he said, any decision to introduce nuclear energy must first satisfy several  conditions before it could be considered in the best interest of consumers.
"Nuclear energy is not merely an electricity generation project.
'It is a long-term national commitment involving safety, radioactive waste management, security, emergency preparedness, governance, financing and public confidence for many decades."
He said Malaysia had yet to  address these issues.
He said consumers deserved full transparency on the  cost of nuclear power, who would  bear those costs, how radioactive waste would be managed, what emergency response systems would be in place and who would be accountable if anything went wrong.
He said nuclear reactors could provide stable baseload electricity because they operated continuously regardless of weather conditions.
But it would be misleading to conclude that nuclear energy would automatically lower electricity bills or  reduce government spending on energy subsidies, he said.
"Consumers should look at the entire life-cycle cost, not only the cost of producing electricity."
He added that nuclear projects required high upfront investments, lengthy construction periods, financing costs, specialised workforce development, security infrastructure, insurance, decommissioning and long-term radioactive waste management.
"These costs  have to be paid by someone,  either taxpayers, electricity consumers or future generations."
He said Malaysia should first maximise energy efficiency and renewable energy before committing to one of the most expensive and complex energy technologies in the world.
Sahabat Alam Malaysia president Meena Raman said nuclear power was inherently unsafe and should not be treated as a clean or green solution for Malaysia.
She said nuclear waste remained radioactive for thousands of years, while nuclear plants were vulnerable to natural disasters, accidents, human error, sabotage and security threats.
"Nuclear energy is an expensive diversion from the task of developing and deploying renewable energy, energy efficiency and the more decentralised energy systems required for a low-carbon future."
She claimed nuclear power would make Malaysia energy insecure as the country would depend on foreign technology and the supply of nuclear material.
She said Malaysia could reduce carbon emissions more cheaply and effectively through renewable energy, energy conservation and energy efficiency measures, instead of choosing nuclear
power and passing the cost to the public.

Title: Hormuz tensions reignite Malaysia's nuclear energy debate
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:  The  tensions around the Strait of Hormuz have intensified fears in global energy markets. For Malaysia, this has revived a harder question over the security of its future power supply.
The concern is not only whether oil and gas prices rise during a crisis, but whether Malaysia's electricity system can remain resilient if it continues to rely  on fossil fuels exposed to external supply risks.
Malaysian Nuclear Agency director-general Dr Muhammad Rawi Mohamed Zin said the  geopolitical uncertainty had disrupted global oil and gas supply chains, affecting Malaysia's energy security.
He said Malaysia's electricity generation system remains  dependent on natural gas and coal, both of which were exposed to supply disruption and global price volatility.
"Nuclear energy is not merely a technological option, but a strategic instrument to strengthen energy security, make Malaysia's electricity supply more resilient and sustainable and reduce exposure to external crises," he told the
New Straits Times
.
He said nuclear power offered a more resilient option as nuclear fuel did not require frequent shipments compared with fossil fuels.
He said uranium's high energy density meant a small amount of fuel could generate electricity over a long period, while fuel stocks could
be stored years in advance to reduce supply risks during conflicts.
He said nuclear power plants could also operate continuously as baseload power for the main grid, making them relevant to Malaysia's long-term industrial and climate planning.
"Nuclear energy is capable of becoming a pillar of stability for the electricity supply system in dealing with Malaysia's increasing electricity demand."
His remarks come amid renewed attention on nuclear energy, after International Atomic Energy Agency director-general Rafael Mariano Grossi said Malaysia was well-positioned to pursue a nuclear power programme due to its long-standing expertise and experience operating a research reactor.
On July 15, Deputy Energy Transition and
Water Transformation Minister Datuk Seri Abdul Rahman Mohamad told the Dewan Rakyat that Malaysia remains at the study stage on nuclear energy and has not committed to any partner country despite reports suggesting otherwise.
He said Malaysia was engaging with multiple countries that had expressed interest in its nuclear programme, including France, Russia and China, but no decision had been made yet.
Prime Minister's Office senior economic adviser  Nurhisham Hussein had said nuclear energy was "the way to go" for Peninsular Malaysia's baseload electricity needs, as solar power could not provide stable baseload supply and the peninsula lacked the hydropower capacity available in Sabah and Sarawak.
Dr Rawi said Malaysia's energy debate should not be limited to whether nuclear power would immediately lower electricity tariffs.
He said the larger question was whether the country could keep electricity prices more predict-able over the long term while supporting data centres, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and other high-load industries.
He added that gas and coal were highly dependent on global market prices, where any rise in fuel prices would increase generation costs and place pressure on government subsidies or consumer tariffs.
"For nuclear power, construction costs are high at the initial stage.
"However, after the plant operates, fuel costs are stable for decades, making nuclear generation less exposed to global price uncertainty."
Dr Rawi said this made nuclear energy relevant not only to power generation, but also to Malaysia's  economic competitiveness.
He said future investors would need confidence that Malaysia could provide reliable, stable and lower-carbon electricity at scale, especially as more economies tightened carbon-related trade and investment expectations.
Beyond energy security, he said, nuclear energy could reduce Malaysia's dependence on fossil fuels, support its climate commitments and provide reliable electricity for high-tech industries.
He said any future plant site would have to meet strict scientific and engineering criteria, with safety, public acceptance, emergency preparedness and transparent communication among the  priorities.
He said any move towards nuclear power should be viewed against Malaysia's need for a secure, diversified and long-term energy mix, rather than the expectation of immediate tariff cuts.
"The goal for Malaysia is to ensure safe, stable and affordable electricity supply for future generations."

Title: Tunisia's Sidi Bou Said inscribed on UNESCO World Heritage list
Article:
TUNIS: Tunisia's coastal city of Sidi Bou Said, famed for its blue and white houses, has been inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List, the organisation said Saturday.
"New inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List: Village of Sidi Bou Saïd," the UN organisation said in a social media post, following a meeting of its committee in South Korea.
A major tourist stop, Sidi Bou Said is known for its winding cobbled roads and blooming bougainvillea, but its beauty is at risk after extreme rainfall last winter.
The Tunisian ministry of cultural affairs hailed the announcement as a signal of "the universal exceptional value of Sidi Bou Said as a space of cultural, spiritual and artistic inspiration."
The village was built in the 18th century around the shrine of the Sufi master Sidi Bou Said.
It nonetheless faces major challenges, including pressure on land use and a need for restoration.
In January, Sidi Bou Said saw its heaviest rainfall in nearly 70 years, causing major damage as mud swept down alleyways, destroying facades and damaging homes.

Title: Once a DAP stronghold, Chennah now a key battleground [WATCH]
Article:
SEREMBAN:  On paper, Chennah appears to be one of DAP's safest seats in Negri Sembilan.
DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke has held the seat comfortably since 2013, transforming what was once an MCA strong-hold into a Pakatan Harapan fortress.
However,   political analysts believe it will be closer for Loke in the Aug 1 polls than in previous elections.
Chennah is among Negri Sembilan's more balanced constituencies, with Malays making up 46 per cent of the electorate and Chinese voters accounting for 44 per cent.
With no single community holding an outright majority, victory will depend on candidates appealing across ethnic and political lines rather than relying  on traditional support bases.
Loke enters the race with significant advantages.
As transport minister, he has the ability to draw federal attention to the  constituency's needs.
His electoral record also reflects sustained voter confidence. In the 2023 state election, Loke retained Chennah with 5,888 votes, defeating Perikatan Nasional by a majority of about 2,200 votes.
This time, however, the electoral understanding between Barisan Nasional and PN is expected to consolidate opposition votes behind MCA candidate Siow Kong Choon, potentially making Chennah far more competitive than three years ago.
But, PN supporters may not automatically back an MCA candidate, just as some traditional BN voters may be uneasy with the new arrangement.
Rather than challenging Loke's national stature, Siow has centred his campaign on accessibility. Loke's responsibilities as a federal minister inevitably leave him with less time for constituency matters.
Siow has used this to position himself as a representative who can devote his full attention to local issues and remain  available to residents.
The message is aimed at voters who view   assemblymen as primarily  responsible for addressing everyday concerns.
State elections often revolve more around local development, municipal issues and constituency service than national politics.
But, Loke's supporters argue that his federal influence is   what benefits Chennah.
They contend his ability to work directly with ministries helps improve coordination between state and federal agencies.
The campaign, therefore, presents voters with a  choice: local accessibility or national influence.
DAP's core support is expected to remain intact, but Loke must convince swing voters that his national responsibilities have not diminished his commitment to local issues.
Asked about Chennah's reputation as one of the election's most closely watched contests, Loke said: "Every seat is a hot seat. Which election isn't competitive? We will continue campaigning calmly and positively."
He said his campaign, now in its second week, had been encouraging.
"We are adopting different approaches in different areas, including reaching out to village communities and holding  meetings. With a week of campaigning remaining, we will continue to campaign positively."
As for Siow, the contest remains an uphill battle.
While MCA is expected to retain much of its traditional support, his chances will also depend on whether PN supporters are willing to back a BN candidate.
BN chairman Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi identified Chennah and neighbouring Linggi as key battlegrounds, saying victories in both seats would strengthen BN's bid to reclaim Negri Sembilan from PH.
Such remarks  reflect the strategic concern now  attached to constituencies once regarded as relatively secure.
Loke responded by saying: "As partners in the cabinet, there's no need to be arrogant. We should campaign positively. Whether someone gets defeated or not is up to the people. The voters will make the decision."
The outcome in Chennah may   hinge on whether the BN-PN electoral understanding   translates into their supporters coming together to vote for Siow on polling day.
If they do not, Loke is likely to extend DAP's dominance.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Kazakh leader tells Putin war should end, Ukraine launches fresh strikes
Article:
MOSCOW: Ukrainian drones struck a Siberian oil refinery in a fresh wave of strikes Saturday, as Kazakhstan's president told Russia's Vladimir Putin the Ukraine war should end during a forum in Siberia's Omsk.
In occupied Ukraine, Russian-installed authorities said a Ukrainian strike had killed 12 people at a seaside "tourist camp", as well as one more in a Moscow-held town and two in Russian border villages.
Kyiv said Russian attacks had killed five people in eastern and southern Ukraine, and two crew members were missing after a Russian strike on a cargo ship carrying corn.
The deaths come as the UN has warned of civilians dying in larger numbers recently in the almost 4.5-year war.
Moscow said Ukraine – which has intensified its retaliatory strikes – launched more than 300 drones into Russia Saturday, including on far-flung regions.
The governor of Siberia's Tyumen region said a local oil refinery had been set ablaze. Russia's athletics federation said an all-Russian competition in the Urals city of Yekaterinburg had been halted over drone threats.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed the Siberia strike and said Kyiv had hit a military factory in the Kirov region for a second day in a row, a day after local authorities said an attack there had killed five people.
Kyiv has said its retaliatory strikes are aimed at damaging Moscow's war effort and forcing the Kremlin to negotiate.
'YOUNG PEOPLE ARE DYING'
In Siberia's Omsk hours after the strikes, Kazakh leader Kassym-Jomart Tokayev told Putin the Ukraine war should end as the pair met for a Russia-Kazakh summit.
"It is a shame, young people are dying... All this has to be stopped," Tokayev said sitting next to Putin in televised comments.
Putin is rarely confronted with officials publicly telling him the fighting should stop.
Tokayev said the conflict should be "frozen" and suggested a return to Istanbul talks before moving "to a long-awaited peace."
The Central Asian leader, who is a Moscow ally but who has never condoned Russia's offensive, said the roots of the war are "not understandable."
Putin responded that he would inform Tokayev on "the details" of the war.
The Russian leader has repeatedly said Moscow intends to take the rest of east Ukraine by force.
US-led talks to end Europe's worst conflict since WWII have stalled.
12 KILLED IN OCCUPIED TOWN
Russian occupational authorities in southern Ukraine said a Ukrainian strike Saturday on the Azov Sea town of Kyrylivka killed 12 people, including four children, accusing Kyiv of having targeted a "tourist camp."
"The whereabouts of eight people is unknown and rescue operations are ongoing," said Yevgeny Balitsky, the Kremlin-installed head of the Russian-occupied part of the Zaporizhzhia region.
Another person was killed in the occupied part of the Kherson region, Moscow said.
Kyiv has not yet commented on the strike, but Ukraine has increased its attacks in the Azov Sea, where it has targeted Russian shipping.
Zelenskyy said a Russian strike on the north-eastern town of Sumy had killed three people at a site belonging to the Nova Poshta private courier service.
Two other people were also killed in southern and eastern Ukraine, Kyiv said.
Kyiv's transport minister Mykola Kalashnyk said on Telegram that Russia had twice hit a civilian vessel carrying almost 2,800 tons of corn as it left the port of Odesa Saturday.
The ship caught fire and seven crew members and a Ukrainian pilot had to be rescued, but two other crew members were missing, he added.
URALS, SIBERIA HIT
Far from the battlefield, Ukrainian drones disrupted an all-Russian athletics competition in the Urals city of Yekaterinburg.
Also in Yekaterinburg, Russian online retail giant Wildberries said it had evacuated its staff over a drone threat, but said its facility had not been damaged.
Wildberries – Russia's version of Amazon – has been targeted by Kyiv's drones for a week, attacks that have killed some workers and caused major fires.
Ukrainian drones have caused nationwide fuel shortages and disrupted ordinary life in Russia more than at any point during more than four years of war.
Russia said Saturday it would extend a fuel export ban until the end of the year.

Title: Wildfires send nearly 260,000 fleeing in France and Spain
Article:
BORDEAUX: Unchecked wildfires raging Saturday in France's southwest and near Spain's capital Madrid have forced nearly 260,000 people to flee and prompted Paris to deploy its military.
France initially hustled 197,000 people from areas around popular vacation spot Bordeaux – one of its biggest-ever peacetime evacuations, though 3,000 were later allowed to return.
In Spain, where 60,000 people were evacuated from villages west of Madrid, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the priority was "to save lives" as he visited the fire zone.
In the Spanish town of Brunete, west of Madrid, mayor Mar Nicolas told AFP she was "very worried."
"Every year there are fires, but this one has been tremendous," she said. "It is a catastrophe."
A separate wildfire near the eastern Spanish city of Valencia killed one person before firefighters brought it under control.
Overstretched firefighters in Spain and France battling around the clock for days have been unable to contain the infernos, which also claimed the lives of two French firefighters near Bordeaux earlier this week.
Earlier Saturday, authorities in both countries suggested the intensity of some of the blazes had lessened.
But the battles were far from won.
The forecasts in France are "turning unfavourable again", Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu warned in a post on X Saturday evening, adding that coming hours "could be difficult."
Spain's Sanchez warned: "We are going to have some complex hours ahead."
Jacqueline Villafranca, a 38-year-old who evacuated to Madrid on Friday, said that when smoke filled her village of Navalagamella "I thought everything was going to burn, the house and everything.
"Here you can breathe normally – yesterday it was unbearable," she said, sitting in a gymnasium-turned-shelter.
TINDERBOX CONDITIONS
The fires in Spain and France advanced quickly because of tinderbox conditions worsened by successive heatwaves the two countries have experienced since May.
Scientists say global warming is increasing droughts and causing weather emergencies to become more extreme and more frequent. Europe is the fastest-warming continent due to climate change.
Both countries were receiving EU help in the form of firefighting aircraft from other European countries.
[[nid:1497090]]
France has deployed 1,500 soldiers and 1,700 security personnel to help firefighters near Bordeaux, and on Saturday an A400M military transport aircraft joined the fleet of smaller planes already dousing flames.
Dozens of firefighters were deployed from Paris to boost the fight. Lecornu said a total of 1,400 firefighters were tackling the blazes.
Local authorities set up emergency shelters in schools and gymnasiums in southwestern France for tourists and residents left wondering what they would return to.
Nuala Kelly, a 75-year-old Irish tourist, said she had never seen anything like this.
"Never, never, never, never, never, and I've travelled all over the world and been in all sorts of situations," she told AFP at Bordeaux's vast exhibition centre now housing thousands of people.
Olivier Stewart, a 38-year-old Frenchman who had to leave the village of Merignac with his wife and young children, said the children were "the most stressed."
"They think the fire is going to burn down the house, but we're coping," he said.
Sunday's final stage of the Tour de France road cycling race has been shortened after the interior ministry said it would need to redeploy officers mobilised for race security to the fires instead.
Lecornu also said that plans were being made "for pets left behind in homes."
'RECORD' AREA BURNT
The massive smoke clouds thrown up by the French and Spanish fires were starting to connect in the atmosphere, according to satellite images from Spain's Aemet weather agency.
Fires currently raging across France have burned nearly 98,000 hectares (242,000 acres) – a "historic record", Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.
In the southwest alone, the flames have consumed more than 32,000 hectares – three times the surface area of Paris – and destroyed at least 100 buildings, authorities said.
French President Emmanuel Macron said the country "will rebuild."
The blazes west of Madrid have burned up to 25,000 hectares, according to Spain's interior ministry.
Two of the three major wildfires there have merged into one, and are threatening to join up to form a massive inferno just kilometres from the capital.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: PN launches six-pillar manifesto for Negri Sembilan election
Article:
SEREMBAN: Perikatan Nasional yesterday launched its manifesto outlining six main pillars for the Negri Sembilan election.
Themed "PN Sepakat Hebatkan Negri Sembilan", the manifesto was launched by PN chairman Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar.
The six pillars focus on governance, youth and family, the economy, social welfare, education and employment.
Early voting for the Negri Sembilan election will take place this Tuesday (July 28), with polling day scheduled for Aug 1.

Title: Sanusi's statement cannot be taken lightly - Azalina
Article:
SEREMBAN: Kedah Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Muhammad Sanusi Mohd Nor's remarks that "the Chinese have China, the Indians have India, the Cambodians have Cambodia, and the Malays only have Malaysia" should not be taken lightly.
Umno information chief Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said said such rhetoric creates the impression that Malaysians of Chinese and Indian descent have another homeland, while suggesting that only Malays truly belong to Malaysia.
"The reality is that for millions of Malaysians of Chinese and Indian descent, Malaysia is not a place of transit. Malaysia is their homeland.
"The Federal Constitution establishes the position of Islam, the institution of the Malay Rulers, and the rights of Malays and Bumiputera. The same Constitution also guarantees the legitimate rights and status of every citizen regardless of their ancestry," she said in a statement today.
Azalina, who is also minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Law and Institutional Reform), said every legitimate citizen shares the same homeland, is protected by the same Constitution and has the right to live in peace and dignity.
Amid the heated campaign for the 16th Negri Sembilan state election, she said all leaders and political campaign machinery must be responsible for every word they utter.
"Issues involving race, religion and the royal institution should not be used as tools to incite anger or fear for the purpose of gaining votes," she said.
She said the people of Negri Sembilan deserved an election campaign focused on issues that genuinely affect their lives, such as the cost of living, employment opportunities, housing, education, healthcare, local development and their children's future.
Azalina said Barisan Nasional did not need fear-based politics to gain support, but instead offered stability, experience, moderation and a nation that provides a place for every citizen.
Sanusi, however, had insisted that his remarks on
Tanah Melayu
being the sole homeland for Malays, made during a ceramah in Negri Sembilan, had been twisted for political gain.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Negri Sembilan polls: BN manifesto not copied from PH, says Zahid
Article:
PORT DICKSON: Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said there was no basis to claim that Barisan Nasional had copied or "copy-pasted" the Pakatan Harapan manifesto for the Negri Sembilan election.
He said the substance of BN's manifesto was not new, but rather the result of the party's continuous efforts over many years.
"There is no question of 'copy-pasting' because from 2004 to 2018, we had formulated those manifestos.
"What is being done now is to improve on what already exists," he told reporters after an event with the Indian community here.
Zahid also warned BN's rivals against making baseless accusations merely to gain political mileage.
"We did not view what they did in Johor previously as 'copy-pasting', so they should not accuse us of doing the same thing," he said.
He said BN's main focus now was to continue development agendas that were stalled after the 14th General Election in 2018.
"We share the same objective, which is to continue the agendas that were stalled when BN failed to secure enough seats to form the government in 2018.
"As such, Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan, as the Negri Sembilan BN chairman, certainly has the right to continue this agenda.
"I am confident that he will do so better with the support of the leadership and BN component parties in Negri Sembilan," he said.
It was previously reported that caretaker Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Aminuddin Harun claimed that BN's manifesto, announced yesterday, had largely
imitated
the manifesto or initiatives introduced and implemented by the state PH government under his leadership.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: PM attends Citrawarna 2026 as Malaysia showcases cultural diversity to global visitors
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Citrawarna 2026 drew more than 700 international visitors from 12 countries, with participants from across Asia, Europe and beyond witnessing one of Malaysia's most celebrated cultural showcases under the Visit Malaysia 2026 campaign.
Visitors from China, India, Mauritius, Japan, Vietnam, Indonesia, Singapore, Kazakhstan, Italy, the Netherlands, Switzerland and France attended the event via specially curated travel packages.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim launched the annual cultural showcase at Dataran Merdeka, with the three-day event featuring 3,500 performers representing states, three federal territories and the nation's multicultural communities in its signature Colours of Parade (Citra Perarakan).
The festival commenced with an opening performance, followed by the parade and a post-show performance, watched by spectators along Jalan Raja and at the Sultan Abdul Samad Building (BSAS).
Also present was Tourism, Arts and Culture Minister Datuk Seri Tiong King Sing.
Citrawarna 2026 features four signature experiences: Colours of Parade, Colours of Flavour, Colours of Culture and Colours of Art.
The event includes more than 70 food and beverage offerings, over 20 cultural activity stations, and more than 10 arts and crafts booths throughout the three-day celebration.
Visitors were also invited to participate in hands-on activities, including batik painting, ketupat weaving and traditional culinary demonstrations led by artisans and cultural practitioners.
Contemporary performances were staged by Malaysian artistes including Wani Kayrie, Bulan Asryaff, Dr Soo Wincci, Santesh Kumar, Ernie Zakri, Aina Abdul and Kumpulan Balle-Balle.
This year's edition, themed
Ritma Warisan
, Nadi Nusa dan Bangsa (The Rhythm of Heritage, The Pulse of the Nation and the People), invites visitors to experience the many traditions, colours and stories that continue to shape the nation.

Title: Fear, arrests keep Cambodians quiet decade after critic's murder
Article:
UNION leader Chhim Sithar served two years in prison after going up against the Cambodian government. Today, she is still making her voice heard, but it is getting riskier.
"Freedom in Cambodia has been shrinking and it is very difficult to speak out," she said at a demonstration this month marking 10 years since the murder of Kem Ley, a prominent government critic gunned down in the capital.
"We are really worried," said the 37-year-old, who was jailed after leading a strike at the nation's largest casino, which authorities deemed illegal.
Since Kem Ley's death, former Cambodian leader Hun Sen and his son, Prime Minister Hun Manet, have tightened their grip over the country they have led for more than 40 years.
Cambodia has four times as many political prisoners today as compared to 2016, the year Kem Ley was shot dead in a Phnom Penh cafe.
A popular political commentator, he was killed soon after giving an interview about an investigative report that detailed some of the millions of dollars allegedly amassed by the ruling family.
At the memorial rally outside the site of Kem Ley's murder, Chhim Sithar said she feared being jailed again, but there was a wider issue at stake.
"What we fear more is the loss of our rights," she said.
Cambodia's main opposition party was banned and its leader Kem Sokha jailed the year after Kem Ley was killed, while several independent media outlets have since been shuttered.
The ruling Cambodian People's Party (CPP) swept the two general elections that followed without a viable challenger, making the country a de facto one-party state.
Opposition politician Rong Chhun said civil rights and political freedoms have been reduced to almost zero, adding that while Cambodia still had public intellectuals, no one matched up to Kem Ley.
Cambodians who criticise the government are regularly arrested — whether they are politicians, activists, farmers or tuk-tuk drivers.
Local rights group Licadho has documented at least 125 political prisoners jailed in Cambodia today, up from about 30 in 2016.
Among them are five members of outlawed environmental group Mother Nature imprisoned in 2024 for between six and eight years for plotting against the state, charges condemned by the United Nations and rights campaigners.
Others have faced the same fate as Kem Ley, with veteran opposition politician Lim Kimya shot dead last year while visiting Thailand, allegedly by a hired killer.
The government has denied any role in his murder.
Rights watchdogs have long accused Cambodian authorities of using violence, arrests and the CPP-dominated courts to silence critics.
"Risks can happen anytime if we speak about something that makes politicians unhappy," analyst Meas Nee said.
Meas Nee said that he, too, speaks more cautiously since Kem Ley was killed.
"It is not that we are not speaking about the truth, but we can only speak of the truth between 50 to 60 per cent of the 100 per cent."
In a message, Information Minister Neth Pheaktra said: "Cambodia does not criminalise criticism. The government welcomes constructive, evidence-based criticism, but all organisations must operate transparently, professionally and in accordance with Cambodian law."
Kem Sokha, leader of the court-dissolved opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party, was pardoned in May after serving nearly a decade of a 27-year sentence for treason.
But his political rights, including holding office and voting, remain revoked.
Recent Western aid cuts have meanwhile left non-governmental organisations  that support Cambodian civil society groups floundering.
Licadho's operations director, Am Sam Ath, said it had lost 30 to 35 per cent of its budget after reductions in United States aid under President Donald Trump.
Another group, Politkoffee, held public forums nearly every week in Phnom Penh for more than eight years, providing a rare outlet for young Cambodians to debate politics.
But nowadays it hosts small meetings in a private setting, after the German think tank that hosted them withdrew its support, one Politkoffee membersaid.
The writers are from AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: The tarnished legacy of fired forensic ICC prosecutor Karim Khan
Article:
KARIM Khan will go down in the history of the International Criminal Court (ICC) as the prosecutor who clinched arrest warrants against the leaders of Russia and Israel, but also as the one who "poisoned the atmosphere" in the institution.
Rigour and precision are the watchwords of this 56-year-old British lawyer when it comes to building a case against the alleged perpetrators of the world's most serious crimes.
But the forensic spotlight shifted to Khan himself after a female staffer accused him of sexual assault — allegations he strongly denies — ultimately costing him his job at the ICC.
At his swearing-in ceremony in 2021 as chief prosecutor of the Hague-based court, Khan said the ICC should be judged on its actions: "The proof of the pudding should be in the eating."
And by obtaining arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Hamas leaders, he has shown he does not shy away from controversy.
Before that, he won an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin, which led to Khan being placed on a wanted list in Russia.
The official has courted controversy throughout a career that has included defending former Liberian president Charles Taylor against allegations of war crimes in Sierra Leone.
Other high-profile clients have included Kenyan President William Ruto who faced charges of crimes against humanity at the ICC — a case that was ultimately dropped.
He was also the lawyer for Seif al-Islam, son of the late Libyan leader  Muammar Gaddafi.
Asked about "crossing the floor" — working as both prosecutor and defence — Khan told specialist journal
OpinioJuris
it helps lawyers stay "grounded".
It also prevents "corrosive traits such as thinking that defence counsel is the devil incarnate or that, as a prosecutor, you are doing 'God's work'," he added.
Initially criticised for dithering over atrocities in Gaza, Khan touched off a firestorm by applying for arrest warrants against Netanyahu and Hamas leaders.
Netanyahu called it a "moral outrage of historic proportions" while then US president Joe Biden described Khan's actions as "outrageous".
Even before Khan's applications, senior US Republicans had penned a letter threatening to bar him and his family from the United States, ending ominously, "you have been warned".
In his defence, Khan said: "This is not a witch hunt. It is a forensic process that is expected of us as international prosecutors."
Born in Scotland,  he studied at a private school in northern England, before reading law at King's College London.
He cut his teeth in international law at the former Yugoslav and Rwandan war crimes tribunals from 1997 to 2000, before representing survivors and relatives of victims of Cambodia's 1970s Khmer Rouge regime before a UN-backed court.
Other roles include a stint at the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, based in The Hague, created to try the assassins of former Lebanese prime minister Rafic Hariri in 2005.
With a nod to the arrogance some critics ascribe to him, the ICC selection panel described him as a "charismatic and articulate communicator who is well aware of his achievements".
A member of the minority Ahmadiyya Muslim sect, he often punctuates his speeches with "Inshallah" (God willing).
"Karim Khan seems like a no-nonsense lawyer," Melanie O'Brien, visiting professor in international law at the University of Minnesota, told AFP.
An ICC prosecutor "has to have a certain fortitude because you know you are going to be up against people who don't agree with you and who don't agree with the court in general".
But the vote by ICC members to sack him as prosecutor amid allegations of wrongdoing will tarnish his legacy.
"Even if they are only accusations, it disturbs us and it has poisoned the atmosphere of the court," deputy prosecutor Mandiaye Niang said in December.
The accusations "are out there and that is enough to cast a veil of doubt over what we're doing", he said.
The writer is from AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Tengku Amir Shah, wife welcome baby girl
Article:
SHAH ALAM: The Raja Muda of Selangor, Tengku Amir Shah Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah and his wife Datin Paduka Seri Afzaa Fadini Abdul Aziz today announced the birth of their first child, Tengku Alia Amira Tengku Amir Shah.

Title: Sonam Wangchuk: 59-year-old who rallied India's Gen Z against Modi and won
Article:
INDIAN social activist Sonam Wangchuk may be pushing 60, but he was one of the faces of a "Cockroach" Gen Z movement that managed to oust Prime Minister Narendra Modi's education minister over exam paper leaks, having fasted for 26 days.
Wangchuk, who is widely believed to have inspired the lead character in a Bollywood blockbuster, is best known for campaigning on issues affecting his Himalayan region of Ladakh, bordering China.
But his fast, alongside a sit-in by the youth Cockroach Janta Party, over exam paper leaks that affected millions of students won him a new following among young Indians.
That helped turn the issue into a broader Gen Z movement, piling pressure on Modi and leading on Saturday to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
"IT'S A VICTORY OF DEMOCRACY, direct democracy... straight from the streets," Wangchuk said after Pradhan's resignation, speaking from his hospital bed, having broken his fast only about a day ago.
"It's a victory of peace, patience & perseverance. Congratulations CJP, Gen Z of the nation and thank you all citizens for shedding fear and the fear of fear and rising up from every corner of the nation."
Even before police in Delhi moved him to hospital a week ago after his hunger strike, some were comparing Wangchuk to India's independence hero Mahatma Gandhi.
He had received video and text messages of support from across India, including from Bollywood actors.
"I am no Gandhi, no hero," he said while fasting.
"I'm just an ordinary citizen who has not shied away from his responsibilities. Don't look for a hero in others. Be the hero of your own life and fulfill your responsibilities."
[[nid:1497037]]
Lovingly called "Sonam Sir" — Sonam means "merit" or "virtue" in some cultures — by many, including CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, Wangchuk is one of Ladakh's most prominent public figures, having built a career around education reform and water-conservation projects in the high-altitude desert.
In 2018, he was awarded the Ramon Magsaysay Award, widely known as Asia's Nobel Prize, for those efforts.
Born in 1966 in the small, remote village of Ulaytokpo in Ladakh, he was a 19-year-old engineering student at the government-run National Institute of Technology in Kashmir when he ran a coaching programme in basic subjects such as English and mathematics that helped hundreds of students. He later set up the Students' Educational and Cultural Movement of Ladakh.
As climate change affected water supplies, Wangchuk built artificial glaciers in the form of "ice stupas", conically shaped ice mountains that store water in winter and melt in summer to supply irrigation water, his Magsaysay citation says.
In recent years, he has become a leading advocate for environmental protection and greater autonomy for Ladakh, a federally controlled territory.
He was jailed for nearly six months in 2025 after deadly protests demanding statehood for the region. Wangchuk denied instigating the violence.
Indian media reported that his father, Sonam Wangyal, was a minister in the former state of Jammu and Kashmir and that former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi helped break one of his hunger strikes over demands for affirmative action for Ladakh residents.
Wangchuk is married to Gitanjali J. Angmo, who also works in education, and has previously said he was prepared to die for his causes.
"FROM ACCOUNTABILITY, NOW TO REFORMS," Wangchuk said on Saturday, flashing a victory sign from his hospital bed, dressed in a striped gown, an ID band on his wrist.
* The writers are from Reuters
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Man held for allegedly assaulting, threatening Ipoh City Council enforcement officer
Article:
IPOH: A 42-year-old man has been arrested for allegedly assaulting and threatening an Ipoh City Council (MBI) enforcement officer while the latter was issuing a compound notice in Pengkalan here yesterday.
District police chief Assistant Commissioner Muhammad Najib Hamzah said the man was detained about 12.40pm today.
He said the incident occurred at Jalan Pengkalan Barat 35 when the enforcement officer was carrying out his duties.
"The man is believed to have acted aggressively by attempting to ram the victim with a vehicle before following him, grabbing him by the collar and issuing threats.
"As a result of the incident, the victim sustained minor injuries and lodged a police report," he said in a statement.
The case is being investigated under Section 353 of the Penal Code for using criminal force against a public servant in the execution of his duties, which carries a maximum two-year jail term or a fine of up to RM10,000, or both, upon conviction.
The case is also being investigated under Section 506 of the Penal Code for criminal intimidation, which carries a maximum two-year jail term or a fine, or both, upon conviction.
He added that police would seek a remand order to facilitate investigations.
Najib warned that stern action would be taken against anyone who obstructs, assaults  or threatens public servants while they are carrying out their official duties.

Title: NST Leader: How syndicates became global enterprises
Article:
FOR those who have been wondering why organised crime syndicates are ubiquitous, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) has an answer.
According to a new report by the UNODC released in Bangkok on Tuesday, once locally rooted syndicates have merged into a single transnational, tech-driven criminal economy sophisticated enough to outpace conventional law enforcement.
In the words of UNODC Regional Representative for Southeast Asia and the Pacific Delphine Schantz, "their operating model looks like corporate franchising" with "specialised departments for laundering money, trafficking people, smuggling migrants and harvesting data, all plugged into the same, service-based interconnected network".
The syndicates are not only outpacing enforcement, but they can teach business schools a thing or two.
The report, titled "An Interconnected Criminal Ecosystem: Transnational Organised Crime Threat Assessment for Southeast Asia 2026", reveals how syndicates in the region are shifting from trafficking physical goods to selling services such as cyber-enabled fraud, criminal infrastructure and platform-based financial settlements that are hard to seize or attribute to any single actor.
Transnational Crime Inc is perhaps the best way to capture the explosive growth of Southeast Asian organised crime syndicates spreading their tentacles, corporate-like, globally.
Like transnational corporations (TNCs), they are beginning to expand their reliance on external service providers. Like TNCs, they, too, choose where they operate.
Syndicates favour countries with weak enforcement or ones where corruption is prevalent. Should governments come under international pressure — like Cambodia is by the United States — the syndicates are nimble enough to shift  their operations.
Little wonder, they are many steps ahead of national policing.
What does all this mean for governments which are serious about curbing  transnational organised crime?
The obvious answer is they have to reimagine enforcement from policing within borders to beyond. For sure, there are already several international pacts. But here, too, organised criminal networks have outpaced treaties.
A prominent one is the United Nations Convention on Transnational Organised Crime. Asean, too, has a pact that allows information sharing and joint operations among its 11 member countries.
But the fact that transnational organised crime is very much around speaks of limited success of such treaties. Some countries just do not have the political will to go after such labyrinthine networks.
Others lack resources. Yet others, being undermined by corruption, are unable to move forward. A new way of seeing the rapidly evolving transnational criminal ecosystem is needed.
For too long, countries around the region have concentrated on disrupting the syndicates. It hasn't worked.
To borrow the words of Albert Einstein, it will be insane to do the same thing over and over again and expect different results.
Something more that includes prevention must be part of the reimagined strategy.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Modi's education minister quits as Indian youth protesters claim victory, end protest
Article:
NEW DELHI: Indian youth protesters called off weeks of demonstrations and celebrated in the streets on Saturday after the education minister quit and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government bowed to demands including calls to fix a cheating-prone exam system.
The worst political crisis of Modi's third term in office had peaked this week when thousands of protesters marched on parliament, with police using tear gas to control them.
Young voters form a critical base of his Bharatiya Janata Party. But youths calling themselves "cockroaches" had taken to the streets since late June, after national exam papers were leaked forcing a resit which affected two million students and galvanised anger about the lack of prospects for young Indians.
The resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, the students' primary demand, came as a surprise because Modi has a reputation for refusing to act under pressure.
Modi's party faces key state elections next year. Similar youth-led protest movements brought down governments in neighbouring Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh in recent years.
Celebrations erupted at the Jantar Mantar protest site in the capital Delhi, with thousands of youngsters chanting victory slogans and dancing.
The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, which spearheaded the demonstrations, said it would end its protests.
"We have done it," said Abhijeet Dipke, CJP's founder, to loud cheers at the site.
Youngsters shouted "Jai Hind", a patriotic slogan meaning "Victory to India", as the national anthem played on loudspeakers and sweets were distributed.
Roads around the central business district of Connaught Place near the protest site were shut amid celebrations and a swelling crowd of thousands of protesters.
Health Minister J.P. Nadda and Jitendra Singh, a junior minister in Modi's office, held a joint press conference with two CJP spokespersons after another round of talks following Pradhan's resignation.
Nadda said the government had accepted all demands of the protesters, which included reforms in the exam system, dropping police cases filed against protesters and compensating families of students who died by suicide after the exam paper leaks.
"The Cockroach Janta Party declares that we withdraw the agitation in good faith," CJP spokesperson Saurav Das said.
"All the demands raised by our team have been accepted, therefore we request protesters to withdraw and peacefully go home," spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka added.
[[nid:1497022]]
"The bottom line is we have won, your struggle, hard work, and patience have paid off," Ranka told cheering crowds at Jantar Mantar on returning from the talks, and urged them to withdraw peacefully.
Opposition parties had echoed the demands of the youth and disrupted the monsoon session of parliament for the entire week, threatening key legislation planned by the government.
Scenes of police using tear gas to control protesters had also fuelled public anger, although authorities defended their actions saying they were only enforcing the law.
Pradhan announced his resignation in a post on X.
"Considering the situation that has arisen at Jantar Mantar and across the country, so that anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation ... I have sent my resignation letter to the Prime Minister," Pradhan wrote.
"I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations of the country's youth."
The protesters had demanded his resignation over leaks of the national medical school entrance test paper in May, which led to the cancellation of results and a retest which affected two million students.
The protests also reflected growing anger in India over job scarcity and government accountability.
Pradhan's resignation is "a victory of peace, patience & perseverance," activist Sonam Wangchuk, who was on a hunger strike for 26 days to support the youth movement, wrote on X.
After news of his resignation, federal authorities restored access to the mobile internet around the protest site, after blocking it for most of the week.
Delhi Metro rail stations in and around the area that were closed for much of four days this week were also opened.
"Young generation is here. This is a win for the constitution," protester Tluanga Ralte said, walking with a copy of the Indian constitution at the protest site after Pradhan's resignation.
"We are not a lazy generation."
Pradhan, 57, a senior member of Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the son of a veteran BJP leader, had been education minister since 2021.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Malaysians in Qatar urged to follow security advisories, avoid military areas
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysians in Qatar have been advised to follow security instructions issued by the local authorities and avoid military areas following the latest developments in the Gulf region.
The Embassy of Malaysia in Doha also urged Malaysians to remain vigilant, stay alert to their surroundings, and avoid being influenced by or spreading false information and rumours.
"The embassy will continue to monitor the situation and provide updates from time to time," it said in a notice posted on its official Facebook page on Saturday.
The embassy also advised Malaysians to check the latest flight schedules before travelling from Qatar and to ensure their personal and family information are kept up to date.
"Should you require any assistance or advice, please contact the embassy at +974 3374 6733 or via email at mwdoha@kln.gov.my," the statement said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Illegally parked vehicles disrupt buses, Rapid KL identifies hotspots
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Rapid KL is working with authorities to identify locations frequently affected by traffic obstructions caused by illegally parked vehicles.
This was following an incident that disrupted bus operations along Jalan Ampang.
"Rapid KL is strengthening cooperation with the police and Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) to pinpoint hotspots where vehicles often block bus movement, while stepping up monitoring and enforcement.
"This includes issuing compounds and towing vehicles found obstructing bus lanes, subject to the relevant laws and enforcement agencies' jurisdiction," it said in a statement.
A viral video shows a
Rapid KL bus
on Route 300 (Maluri Depot–Lebuh Ampang) struggling to continue its journey from Jalan Yap Kwan Seng to Jalan Ampang.
The incident, which occurred at about 8.30pm on July 22, was caused by a vehicle parked on the roadside at the Jalan Yap Kwan Seng–Jalan Ampang junction, blocking both the bus and traffic flow.
Rapid KL said the obstruction led to congestion and disrupted bus operations along the route, affecting schedules and passengers' travel experience.
Rapid KL also urged road users to comply with traffic regulations and avoid parking in areas that could obstruct buses, particularly at junctions, bus stops, dedicated bus lanes and other spaces requiring sufficient clearance for public transport.
It said such obstructions not only disrupt services and cause delays but also pose potential safety risks to road users.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Anwar wants Felda initiatives implemented soon, demands monthly progress reports
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim wants seven previously announced initiatives to assist Felda settlers to be implemented soon.
Anwar said he wanted monthly progress reports on all the projects to prevent delays.
"I want monthly reports on all seven projects.
"Sometimes, I do not blame the people. When we make announcements, they become tired of waiting.
"Since they have waited so long for the second house issue, we must resolve it," he said.
On July 7, Anwar announced
seven
incentives for Felda settlers covering housing, digital literacy, education, healthcare initiatives and the welfare of agency staff.
He said the government would establish a dedicated committee to resolve long-standing issues involving second-generation Felda settlers.
On amendments to the Felda Act, Anwar said an initial draft was being finalised before being presented to the board of directors, the Cabinet and eventually Parliament.
"I have given instructions for it to be tabled before the end of this year. But the Act itself is not an obstacle.
"If Felda and the government agree, and state governments do not object, several programmes can proceed even before the Act is finalised."
He added that the Act was being amended to resolve all pending issues legally so they would not be raised again in the future.
"Who knows if there is a new prime minister tomorrow? Many people may propose changes. So, while I am still here, it is better for me to resolve this first," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Push to unveil Tabung Haji RCI report grows
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Experts have called for the immediate release of the Royal Commission of Inquiry (RCI) report on Lembaga Tabung Haji (TH), saying it is necessary to establish the truth, protect depositors and improve the institution's governance.
While supporting greater transparency, senior lecturer in political science at Universiti Teknologi Mara (UiTM) in Seremban, Dr Mazlan Che Soh, said the report should not become a tool for assigning blame before legal proceedings are completed or for pursuing short-term political interests.
"The public, particularly depositors, have a right to know the outcome of the inquiry because TH is not merely a financial institution but a trust institution for Muslims that manages savings for the haj pilgrimage.
"Transparency is essential to address the questions that remain, identify governance shortcomings and ensure such mistakes are not repeated," he told Bernama today.
He said the government should release an executive summary, set out the RCI recommendations that have been acted upon and explain the next steps.
While acknowledging that the report's release could influence the views of some voters, particularly Malay-Muslim voters and TH depositors, Mazlan said it would not necessarily lead to a significant shift in overall public support.
He said voters' decisions were shaped by various factors, including the cost of living, the performance of state governments, candidates' credibility, party loyalty and the strength of grassroots machinery.
Meanwhile, Senior Lecturer in Political Science at the Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities, Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM), Dr Jamaie Hamil, said the TH issue had dragged on for too long, with improvements already made from the first Pakatan Harapan administration to the current Madani government.
Retired civil servant Wan Osman Hashim, 70, said in a video posted on TikTok that the government should act quickly to resolve the issue and ensure justice for the public.
"We want the government to resolve this matter quickly so that Tabung Haji does not suffer losses. The government must take action to ensure people can continue saving with Tabung Haji with sincerity.
"It is crucial to investigate any alleged wrongdoing involving Malaysians' money," he said in the one-minute-eight-second video, which was also shared by Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim expressed confidence that the Cabinet would agree to the proposal to make the RCI report on Tabung Haji public after it is tabled for the Cabinet's consideration.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: BN will 'call the shots' in understanding with PN, says Tok Mat
Article:
SEREMBAN: Barisan Nasional deputy chairman Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan has dismissed concerns that voting for BN would also give influence to Pas through the coalition's understanding with Perikatan Nasional.
He said BN would remain the dominant partner and "call the shots" if entrusted to form the Negri Sembilan government, likening the coalition to a company where the majority shareholder determines its direction.
Responding to concerns circulating on social media, Mohamad said BN's role in the understanding should be viewed through the lens of a company structure, where the majority shareholder determines the organisation's direction.
"If a company is controlled by an 80 per cent shareholder, the remaining 20 per cent shareholder cannot do much.
"In the Negri Sembilan election, we have 25 seats, while Pas and Parti Wawasan Negara together have 11 seats," he said when appearing on Podcast Utama Buletin TV3 in conjunction with the Negri Sembilan election last night.
Mohamad said concerns would only be justified if BN were the minority partner.
"Unless they have 80 per cent and BN only has 20 per cent, then people may have reason to be concerned.
"If we are given the mandate to form the government, we will do so as the majority," he said.
He also pointed out that Pas had publicly stated it had no intention of seeking the menteri besar's post.
"So what is there to worry about?" he said.
Mohamad said the narrative that a vote for BN was effectively a vote for Pas was being amplified on social media to undermine growing support for BN among Chinese voters.
"Chinese voters rarely declare their political preference openly. But now they are openly saying they will support BN.
"There are people who are unhappy about that."
On whether the swing among Chinese voters in Johor could be replicated in Negri Sembilan, Mohamad said the shift reflected long-standing dissatisfaction within the community, particularly among business owners.
He cited issues such as the Sales and Service Tax (SST), e-invoicing requirements and enforcement against overloaded lorries as among the factors that had fuelled discontent.
"The momentum in Johor is real, but the Chinese community has been unhappy for a long time.
"I hope they will translate that in Negri Sembilan as well.
"They have already done so in Johor, and I hope they will do the same in Negri Sembilan so that the problems faced by the community can be properly addressed," he said.

Title: Negri Sembilan polls: BN-PN pact should remain electoral understanding, says Tok Mat
Article:
SEREMBAN: Barisan Nasional's pact with Perikatan Nasional in Negri Sembilan should remain an electoral understanding rather than be turned into a formal coalition, said Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan.
The BN deputy chairman said if the understanding proved to be a workable formula, there would be no need to change it.
"We have reached an understanding first and should move one step at a time. We should not be trying to take two or three steps ahead all at once.
"Don't start sliding before you have even sat down. Jangan berlunjur sebelum duduk. Duduk dulu, baru kita berlunjur (Sit down first, then you can slide).
"Only then can we assess the arrangement's success rate, identify any shortcomings and determine the reasons if it fails to produce the desired outcome.
"We should not immediately abandon what we are doing. There is no need to rush into forming a coalition," he said when appearing on Podcast Utama Buletin TV3 in conjunction with the Negri Sembilan election.
Mohamad, who is also Umno deputy president, said the Malay political landscape had long been party-based, making it unrealistic to unite all Malay-based parties under a single coalition.
He pointed to previous political alliances that eventually broke apart, saying an electoral understanding was a more practical approach.
"It is better for us to have an understanding so that we can avoid contesting against one another.
"If we can achieve that, Alhamdulillah, because one of the main reasons BN lost and Malay politics weakened was due to contests among ourselves.
"How can we place two or three parties with different ideologies and political approaches into one grouping? It cannot be done.
"It can never work. It's not that I'm being overly pessimistic, but it is better for us to maintain an understanding."
Mohamad said such an arrangement would allow each party to retain its identity while continuing to pursue its own policies and cooperate during elections.
"No party is willing to see its identity diluted. We do not want our party to be diluted either," he said.
He added that if the understanding proved successful in Negri Sembilan, it could be replicated elsewhere.
"If it works here, why not continue with the understanding? The important thing is that we can form the government in Negri Sembilan and perhaps in Melaka later," he said.
